screens.title: What AWS WAF protects and how it works
screens.narratorSegment: AWS WAF is a web application firewall that filters HTTP and HTTPS requests to your application or A P I. At its core, WAF evaluates incoming requests against a Web ACL composed of rules and rule groups. Managed rule groups are provided by AWS or Marketplace sellers and protect against common attacks such as S Q L injection and cross-site scripting without writing custom patterns. Custom rules let you filter by IP addresses, headers, body content, and URIs; IP-set rules can block known bad IPs. A practical safety pattern is to deploy managed rule groups and set them to COUNT mode first. COUNT mode records matches without blocking traffic, letting you measure false positives before you enforce BLOCK. WAF can be associated with CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, or A P I Gateway endpoints, so it sits at the edge of your application stack. One common misconception is that WAF replaces secure coding and input validation. It does not; WAF is a mitigation layer that reduces risk and filters obvious exploits, but secure coding practices are still required. Example: adding AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet to an ALB inspects query strings and body payloads for SQLi patterns. Key takeaway: use managed rules to gain coverage quickly, test in COUNT mode, and add narrowly scoped IP-block rules only after validating impact.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.2 › AWS WAF Fundamentals
Core Concept

What AWS WAF protects and how it works

WAF inspects HTTP(S) requests with Web ACLs made of managed and custom rules. It reduces web exploit risk but doesn't replace secure coding.

Managed Rule Groups
Pre-built protections like AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet for SQLi and XSS.
Custom Rules
IP set blocking, header checks, URI filtering. Use narrow scope to avoid false positives.
Deployment Targets
CloudFront, ALB, and API Gateway.
Key Takeaway

WAF is best used with managed rules for coverage and custom rules for precise blocking. Always test rules in COUNT mode before enforcement.

Example: Protect an ALB
Create a Web ACL named MyWebAppProtection, add AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet set to COUNT, and a custom IP-set called BlockBadIPs with a sample entry. Associate the Web ACL with the ALB to begin recording matches. Monitor metrics and logs before switching to BLOCK.
Common Mistake
Flipping rules to BLOCK in production without COUNT-mode validation can cause unintended denial of service to real users.
Pro Tip
Use managed rules to start, then add tight, well-scoped custom rules for IPs or unusual patterns you observe in logs.

screens.title: Deploying a Web ACL safely
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows a safe deployment pattern for a WAF Web ACL. Start by creating a Web ACL in the same region as your ALB and give it a clear name such as MyWebAppProtection. Step two: add a managed rule group like AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and set its action to COUNT. COUNT records matches but does not drop traffic; this prevents accidental outages while you tune rules. Step three: create a custom IP set named BlockBadIPs and add a test IP that you control, for example a proxy you can access. Add a rule that references this IP set and set its action to BLOCK. Give the custom rule a lower priority number so it is evaluated before broader managed rules. Step four: associate the Web ACL with your ALB. Allow traffic and monitor WAF metrics, CloudWatch logs, and ALB access logs. Step five: simulate a blocked request from the test IP and verify it is blocked, and simulate an exploit-pattern request to confirm the managed rule group logs a match in COUNT. Only after validating that legitimate traffic is unaffected should you switch safe managed rules to BLOCK. This pattern reduces disruption and reveals false positives before enforcement.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.2 › Safe WAF Deployment
Process Flow

Deploying a Web ACL safely

Follow a conservative sequence to avoid blocking legitimate traffic while gaining protection visibility.

1. Create Web ACL
Name it clearly and select the region matching your ALB.
2. Add Managed Rule Group (COUNT)
Add AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and set action to COUNT to observe matches only.
3. Add Custom IP Set & Rule
Create BlockBadIPs and add a test IP. Create a rule to BLOCK that IP with higher priority.
4. Associate with ALB and Monitor
Check WAF metrics, ALB logs, and CloudWatch for COUNT matches and blocked events.
5. Validate and Enforce
Once validated, change safe managed rules to BLOCK and keep targeted IP blocks enabled.
Example Scenario
You add a test proxy IP to BlockBadIPs, attempt access from that proxy, and confirm the ALB returns a blocked response while legitimate users remain unaffected. Observe COUNT hits in the WAF metrics to tune rules.
Misconception Check
COUNT mode is not enforcement. It is a measurement tool—do not assume it blocks traffic until you set BLOCK.

screens.title: Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced
screens.narratorSegment: AWS Shield Standard provides automatic, inline detection and mitigation for frequently occurring network and transport layer DDoS attacks. It is enabled for all customers by default and handles many common volumetric or protocol-based attacks without any configuration. Shield Advanced, by contrast, is a paid offering for business-critical applications. It delivers enhanced detection and mitigation for larger or more sophisticated attacks, near real-time visibility into attack details, cost protection against scaling charges caused by an attack, and 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team. That access is important when an attack requires hands-on assistance and tailored mitigations. A common question is whether Shield Advanced replaces WAF. It does not. Shield protects primarily at network and transport layers, while WAF protects the application layer. For an e-commerce platform under persistent volumetric attack, Shield Advanced is the appropriate choice because it provides the DDoS cost protection and DRT escalation paths that Shield Standard lacks. When planning, balance the cost and risk: Shield Advanced is a strategic investment when uptime and unexpected scaling costs pose unacceptable business risk. Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced means shield standard is a free baseline for common attacks; shield advanced adds deep mitigation, drt, and cost protection for high-value targets.. In practical terms, baseline automatic mitigation vs enhanced protection, visibility, and response. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 02 › Chapter 2.2 › Shield Comparison
Comparison

Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced

Understand the scope and when to invest in Shield Advanced for business-critical protections.

Shield Standard
Automatic baseline mitigation for common network and transport DDoS attacks; enabled for all customers.
Shield Advanced
Enhanced mitigation for larger or complex attacks, near real-time visibility, DDoS cost protection, and 24/7 DRT access.
When to use Advanced

Choose Advanced for high-value applications where downtime or scaling costs pose significant business risk, such as critical e-commerce or financial services.

Example
An e-commerce platform experiencing frequent large volumetric attacks would use Shield Advanced to gain cost protection and access to DRT for coordinated mitigation.
Misconception
Shield Advanced is not a substitute for WAF. Use WAF for application-layer filtering and Shield for network/transport protections.
Key Takeaway
Combine WAF for application threats with Shield Advanced for stronger DDoS protections when required by risk tolerance.

screens.title: Centralized policy with AWS Firewall Manager
screens.narratorSegment: Firewall Manager centralizes security policy management across accounts in an AWS Organization. Instead of configuring a WAF Web ACL in twenty separate accounts and risking inconsistent rules, you create a policy in Firewall Manager and it automatically applies to matching resources across accounts, including new resources created later. Firewall Manager supports deployment of WAF rules, Shield Advanced protections, Network Firewall rules, and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rules. This centralized approach reduces operational overhead and helps prevent configuration drift. A practical example: define a Firewall Manager policy that enforces the MyWebAppProtection Web ACL on all ALBs with a specific tag across 15 accounts; Firewall Manager will roll out that Web ACL and remediate non-compliant resources. Beware of scope mistakes—if you define overly broad criteria, you may unintentionally apply rules to resources that do not require them. Always test policies in a subset of accounts or with tags to ensure selective application. Firewall Manager is particularly valuable in multi-account organizations where consistency and scalability of security controls are critical. Centralized policy with AWS Firewall Manager means use firewall manager to deploy and enforce consistent waf and firewall policies across multiple accounts, avoiding drift and manual errors.. In practical terms, apply waf, shield advanced, and firewall policies across multiple accounts and vpcs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.2 › Firewall Manager
Architecture

Centralized policy with AWS Firewall Manager

Firewall Manager allows a single policy to deploy and enforce security controls across an organization, reducing manual work and drift.

Capabilities
  • Deploy WAF Web ACLs and managed rules across accounts
  • Enforce Shield Advanced protections and Network Firewall rules
  • Apply Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rules
Example Policy
Create a policy to enforce MyWebAppProtection on ALBs tagged with environment:production across 15 accounts. Firewall Manager applies the Web ACL and remediates non-compliant ALBs automatically.
Misconception
Firewall Manager does not guess scope—if you choose broad criteria, it will apply broadly. Design selectors carefully.
Why it matters
Consistency reduces risk from human error and simplifies audits and compliance across many accounts.

screens.title: VPC Flow Logs: what they record and why they matter
screens.narratorSegment: VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic to and from network interfaces in your VPC. Each flow log record includes source and destination IP addresses, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, start and end times, the action (ACCEPT or REJECT), and identifiers such as interface and subnet. You can publish flow logs to CloudWatch Logs for near-real-time troubleshooting or to S3 for archival and analysis with Athena. These records are invaluable for security investigations: for example, a high volume of REJECTed outbound connections to unfamiliar IP addresses from a private subnet may indicate data exfiltration attempts or a compromised instance attempting to reach a command-and-control host. A common misconception is that flow logs contain packet payloads; they do not. Flow logs provide metadata only, which supports session analysis without exposing content. To analyze logs quickly, use CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena with parsing queries to filter by action, IP, and ports. Ultimately, VPC Flow Logs give you the visibility needed to detect anomalous network behavior that prevention layers may miss. VPC Flow Logs: what they record and why they matter means use vpc flow logs to trace sessions and spot anomalies, but remember they do not include packet contents.. In practical terms, session-level visibility into source/destination, ports, protocols, bytes, and accept/reject actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 02 › Chapter 2.2 › VPC Flow Logs
Definition

VPC Flow Logs: what they record and why they matter

Flow logs record session metadata for traffic to and from network interfaces, enabling security and compliance analysis.

Fields captured
Source/destination IP, ports, protocol, packets, bytes, start/end, action (ACCEPT/REJECT), interface IDs.
Destinations
Publish to CloudWatch Logs for quick queries or to S3 for longer-term storage and Athena analysis.
Limitations
Flow logs do not contain packet payloads; they provide metadata for session-level analysis only.
Example Investigation
If you see many REJECTed outbound connections from a private subnet to unknown IPs, follow up by identifying the instance, checking processes and open sockets, and correlating with GuardDuty findings.
Key Takeaway

VPC Flow Logs are essential for detecting suspicious session patterns; pair them with GuardDuty for prioritized alerts.

Common Mistake
Expecting payload data from flow logs. Use other tools for packet capture when payloads are required and authorized.

screens.title: Enable VPC Flow Logs and query with CloudWatch Logs Insights
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough shows how to enable VPC Flow Logs and query them to find rejected or suspicious traffic. First, in the VPC console select your VPC and create a flow log with Filter set to All and Destination set to CloudWatch Logs. Choose or create a log group, and ensure the IAM role has permission to publish logs. After a few minutes, flow logs begin populating. To find rejects from a specific IP or to surface REJECT records, use CloudWatch Logs Insights. The example query filters for logStatus OK and action REJECT, parses the message into fields, and filters by the source IP you are testing. Running that query returns recent REJECT events and helps you correlate with WAF blocks or instance behavior. A common trap is not allowing enough time for streams to appear or misconfiguring the IAM role, which results in missing logs. Another is forgetting to set Filter to All when you need both ACCEPT and REJECT for full visibility. Example queries and saved dashboards speed investigations when incidents occur. Enable VPC Flow Logs and query with CloudWatch Logs Insights means enable flow logs early and use cloudwatch logs insights queries to quickly surface rejects and suspicious sessions.. In practical terms, create a flow log, publish to cloudwatch, and run a query to find rejected traffic from a test ip. Module 02 › Chapter 2.2 › Flow Logs & Queries
Process

Enable VPC Flow Logs and query with CloudWatch Logs Insights

Set the flow log filter to All, send to CloudWatch, verify role permissions, then query to find REJECTs or test-IP activity.

Steps
  1. Create flow log for the VPC with Filter = All, Destination = CloudWatch Logs.
  2. Create/choose an IAM role with publish permissions.
  3. Wait for streams, then use Logs Insights to query records.
Example CloudWatch Logs Insights Query
fields @timestamp, @message
| filter logStatus = "OK" and action = "REJECT"
| parse @message "* * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *" as version, account, interfaceid, srcaddr, dstaddr, srcport, dstport, protocol, packets, bytes, start, end, action, logstatus, vpc_id, subnet_id, instance_id, tcp_flags, type, pkts_src_to_dst, pkts_dst_to_src, bytes_src_to_dst, bytes_dst_to_src
| filter srcaddr = '1.1.1.1'
| sort @timestamp desc
Replace the test IP with your bad IP. The parse step maps fields from the raw flow log message for filtering.
Key Takeaway

Validate that streams appear in CloudWatch before relying on queries. Ensure IAM role and Filter settings are correct.

screens.title: Amazon GuardDuty: network-focused findings
screens.narratorSegment: Amazon GuardDuty analyzes multiple data sources—VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events—using machine learning and threat intelligence to detect suspicious activity. GuardDuty generates findings such as PortScan or C&C (command and control) communications that are specifically useful for network investigations. For example, a finding like PenTest:EC2/PortScan indicates an instance is performing port scans; Backdoor:EC2/C&CActivity indicates communication with a known malicious host. GuardDuty reduces manual log triage by prioritizing likely threats and attaching contextual information, such as affected resources and related IP addresses. A useful pattern is to integrate GuardDuty findings with Security Hub or a SIEM so you can centralize alerting and build automated responses for high-fidelity findings. Beware of treating GuardDuty as a replacement for flow log analysis; it augments it by surfacing notable patterns, but investigators should still drill into raw flow logs and instance telemetry for root cause. GuardDuty findings help you focus your attention on the most important network anomalies quickly. Definition

Amazon GuardDuty: network-focused findings

GuardDuty uses ML and threat intelligence to analyze flow, DNS, and CloudTrail data and surface prioritized alerts for investigation.

PenTest:EC2/PortScan, Backdoor:EC2/C&CActivity—each points to network-level suspicious behavior.

screens.title: Putting it together: layered defense architecture
screens.narratorSegment: A robust network security posture uses layered controls that complement one another. Picture the stack: WAF sits at the application perimeter, filtering HTTP(S) for S Q L injection, XSS, and known bad bots. Shield Standard provides automatic network/transport protections; Shield Advanced sits at the same layer but adds deeper mitigation, visibility, DRT access, and cost protection. Firewall Manager orchestrates policy deployment across accounts so that WAF Web ACLs and Shield protections are consistent everywhere. VPC Flow Logs provide the telemetry you need to see session-level behavior across subnets and interfaces. GuardDuty ingests those logs and surfaces prioritized findings that point your investigative effort to the most important events. In practice, protect your ALB with a Web ACL, opt into Shield Advanced for high-value targets, use Firewall Manager to ensure the same Web ACL and Shield settings are applied across accounts, enable VPC Flow Logs to CloudWatch for quick queries, and rely on GuardDuty to alert on anomalies. A misconception is to treat any single service as sufficient; the goal is complementary coverage where each service covers the blind spots of the others.

Module 02 › Chapter 2.2 › Hands-on Activity
Hands-on Activity

Implement WAF Protection and Analyze VPC Flow Logs

Follow the checklist to protect an ALB-backed web app safely and verify behavior using flow logs and WAF metrics.

Checklist
  1. Enable VPC Flow Logs: Filter = All, Destination = CloudWatch Logs, create log group.
  2. Create Web ACL MyWebAppProtection, add AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet in COUNT mode.
  3. Create IP set BlockBadIPs with a controlled test IP and add a BLOCK rule.
  4. Associate Web ACL with ALB and monitor metrics/logs.
  5. Run test requests from the blocked IP and review flow logs and WAF COUNT hits.
Expected Outcome
The test IP is blocked by the IP-set rule; managed rule matches appear as COUNT hits. Flow logs show REJECT for blocked sessions and provide session metadata for follow-up.
Key Takeaway

The safe cycle is observe, tune, then enforce to avoid unintended outages while improving protection.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we'll build a practical mental model for protecting AWS networks and web applications. You will learn what each service—AWS WAF, Shield Standard and Advanced, Firewall Manager, VPC Flow Logs, and GuardDuty—does, how they complement one another, and where to use them in real deployments. We'll look at safe WAF testing patterns, how Shield Advanced extends baseline DDoS protection with cost protection and access to the DDoS Response Team, and how Firewall Manager centralizes policy across accounts. You'll also learn how to enable and interpret VPC Flow Logs to spot suspicious sessions and how GuardDuty turns those logs into prioritized findings. A concrete example ties this together: protecting an EC2-based web app behind an ALB, deploying a WAF Web ACL with managed and IP-block rules, enabling flow logs to CloudWatch, and using GuardDuty to detect anomalies. Along the way we emphasize practical safety: test WAF rules in COUNT mode, verify log ingestion, and confirm Firewall Manager scope before broad enforcement. By the end you'll be able to design a layered network protection posture and run targeted investigations when GuardDuty or flow logs surface suspicious activity.

These objectives guide the hands-on and design work in this chapter. First, you'll evaluate and implement AWS WAF rules to protect web applications from common exploits and automated bots. That means understanding managed rule groups, creating an IP-set block rule, and testing rules safely in COUNT mode so legitimate users aren't blocked. Second, you'll distinguish Shield Standard from Shield Advanced and decide when to use Advanced for high-value applications that need DDoS cost protection and access to the DDoS Response Team. Third, you'll learn to use AWS Firewall Manager to deploy consistent WAF and firewall policies across multiple accounts, preventing configuration drift and reducing operational overhead. Finally, you'll configure VPC Flow Logs, send them to CloudWatch or S3, and use CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena to query traffic records. You will also learn to leverage GuardDuty's network findings to prioritize incidents. Each objective includes hands-on steps and a short verification milestone that ensures you can confirm correct behavior in a test environment.

This chapter is organized to build understanding first, then practice. We'll begin with a clear comparison that separates application-layer protections provided by WAF from network-layer protections supplied by Shield. Next you'll follow a lab-style walkthrough to create a Web ACL, add a managed rule group, and add a custom IP block rule, practicing COUNT mode. After that you'll configure VPC Flow Logs and send them to CloudWatch Logs so you can query traffic and identify rejects or anomalous sessions. We'll show a CloudWatch Logs Insights query example you can reuse. The lesson then covers Firewall Manager: how a single policy can deploy the same WAF rules across multiple accounts and why that reduces misconfiguration risk. Finally, we'll examine GuardDuty's network-focused findings, explain their meaning, and show how to integrate them with a SIEM or Security Hub for centralized response. Each section includes a short misconception check so you can avoid common mistakes such as flipping WAF to BLOCK in production before testing or assuming Shield Standard replaces application-layer filtering.

AWS WAF is a web application firewall that filters HTTP and HTTPS requests to your application or A P I. At its core, WAF evaluates incoming requests against a Web ACL composed of rules and rule groups. Managed rule groups are provided by AWS or Marketplace sellers and protect against common attacks such as S Q L injection and cross-site scripting without writing custom patterns. Custom rules let you filter by IP addresses, headers, body content, and URIs; IP-set rules can block known bad IPs. A practical safety pattern is to deploy managed rule groups and set them to COUNT mode first. COUNT mode records matches without blocking traffic, letting you measure false positives before you enforce BLOCK. WAF can be associated with CloudFront distributions, Application Load Balancers, or A P I Gateway endpoints, so it sits at the edge of your application stack. One common misconception is that WAF replaces secure coding and input validation. It does not; WAF is a mitigation layer that reduces risk and filters obvious exploits, but secure coding practices are still required. Example: adding AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet to an ALB inspects query strings and body payloads for SQLi patterns. Key takeaway: use managed rules to gain coverage quickly, test in COUNT mode, and add narrowly scoped IP-block rules only after validating impact.

This walkthrough shows a safe deployment pattern for a WAF Web ACL. Start by creating a Web ACL in the same region as your ALB and give it a clear name such as MyWebAppProtection. Step two: add a managed rule group like AWSManagedRulesCommonRuleSet and set its action to COUNT. COUNT records matches but does not drop traffic; this prevents accidental outages while you tune rules. Step three: create a custom IP set named BlockBadIPs and add a test IP that you control, for example a proxy you can access. Add a rule that references this IP set and set its action to BLOCK. Give the custom rule a lower priority number so it is evaluated before broader managed rules. Step four: associate the Web ACL with your ALB. Allow traffic and monitor WAF metrics, CloudWatch logs, and ALB access logs. Step five: simulate a blocked request from the test IP and verify it is blocked, and simulate an exploit-pattern request to confirm the managed rule group logs a match in COUNT. Only after validating that legitimate traffic is unaffected should you switch safe managed rules to BLOCK. This pattern reduces disruption and reveals false positives before enforcement.

AWS Shield Standard provides automatic, inline detection and mitigation for frequently occurring network and transport layer DDoS attacks. It is enabled for all customers by default and handles many common volumetric or protocol-based attacks without any configuration. Shield Advanced, by contrast, is a paid offering for business-critical applications. It delivers enhanced detection and mitigation for larger or more sophisticated attacks, near real-time visibility into attack details, cost protection against scaling charges caused by an attack, and 24/7 access to the AWS DDoS Response Team. That access is important when an attack requires hands-on assistance and tailored mitigations. A common question is whether Shield Advanced replaces WAF. It does not. Shield protects primarily at network and transport layers, while WAF protects the application layer. For an e-commerce platform under persistent volumetric attack, Shield Advanced is the appropriate choice because it provides the DDoS cost protection and DRT escalation paths that Shield Standard lacks. When planning, balance the cost and risk: Shield Advanced is a strategic investment when uptime and unexpected scaling costs pose unacceptable business risk. Shield Standard vs Shield Advanced means shield standard is a free baseline for common attacks; shield advanced adds deep mitigation, drt, and cost protection for high-value targets.. In practical terms, baseline automatic mitigation vs enhanced protection, visibility, and response. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Firewall Manager centralizes security policy management across accounts in an AWS Organization. Instead of configuring a WAF Web ACL in twenty separate accounts and risking inconsistent rules, you create a policy in Firewall Manager and it automatically applies to matching resources across accounts, including new resources created later. Firewall Manager supports deployment of WAF rules, Shield Advanced protections, Network Firewall rules, and Route 53 Resolver DNS Firewall rules. This centralized approach reduces operational overhead and helps prevent configuration drift. A practical example: define a Firewall Manager policy that enforces the MyWebAppProtection Web ACL on all ALBs with a specific tag across 15 accounts; Firewall Manager will roll out that Web ACL and remediate non-compliant resources. Beware of scope mistakes—if you define overly broad criteria, you may unintentionally apply rules to resources that do not require them. Always test policies in a subset of accounts or with tags to ensure selective application. Firewall Manager is particularly valuable in multi-account organizations where consistency and scalability of security controls are critical. Centralized policy with AWS Firewall Manager means use firewall manager to deploy and enforce consistent waf and firewall policies across multiple accounts, avoiding drift and manual errors.. In practical terms, apply waf, shield advanced, and firewall policies across multiple accounts and vpcs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. VPC Flow Logs capture metadata about IP traffic to and from network interfaces in your VPC. Each flow log record includes source and destination IP addresses, ports, protocol, packet and byte counts, start and end times, the action (ACCEPT or REJECT), and identifiers such as interface and subnet. You can publish flow logs to CloudWatch Logs for near-real-time troubleshooting or to S3 for archival and analysis with Athena. These records are invaluable for security investigations: for example, a high volume of REJECTed outbound connections to unfamiliar IP addresses from a private subnet may indicate data exfiltration attempts or a compromised instance attempting to reach a command-and-control host. A common misconception is that flow logs contain packet payloads; they do not. Flow logs provide metadata only, which supports session analysis without exposing content. To analyze logs quickly, use CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena with parsing queries to filter by action, IP, and ports. Ultimately, VPC Flow Logs give you the visibility needed to detect anomalous network behavior that prevention layers may miss. Amazon GuardDuty analyzes multiple data sources—VPC Flow Logs, DNS logs, and CloudTrail events—using machine learning and threat intelligence to detect suspicious activity. GuardDuty generates findings such as PortScan or C&C (command and control) communications that are specifically useful for network investigations. For example, a finding like PenTest:EC2/PortScan indicates an instance is performing port scans; Backdoor:EC2/C&CActivity indicates communication with a known malicious host. GuardDuty reduces manual log triage by prioritizing likely threats and attaching contextual information, such as affected resources and related IP addresses.
